items.title: A cupboard of different substances
items.student: Fictional school-store case: labelled vinegar is sour, a bicarbonate solution is mildly basic, and one stored salt has become wet while washing-soda crystals have become powdery. These descriptions are a puzzle, not an instruction to taste or touch. Predict whether one explanation can account for all changes. During the unit, build a “Substance–evidence–explanation–safe use” chart.
items.teacher: Keep three questions distinct: aqueous acidity/basicity, chemical reactions, and water exchange between salts and air. Do not assume every salt is neutral or behaves identically. The school-store case is invented; observations during class must be recorded honestly, including no visible change.

items.title: Indicator investigation
items.student: Materials per group: labelled wells with 1 mL each of food vinegar diluted 1: 4 with water, dilute sodium bicarbonate solution prepared by the teacher (1 g in 100 mL water), and distilled water; universal-indicator paper and its manufacturer’s chart; separate droppers; goggles. Put one drop on separate indicator strips, compare with the chart and record an approximate pH and classification. Never return a dropper to another sample. Repeat one measurement. If strips are unavailable, analyse this explicitly illustrative evidence: vinegar pH3, bicarbonate pH8, water pH7.
items.teacher: Actual results depend on sample, water, concentration and indicator range; the illustrative values are not mandatory class results. For these aqueous samples near room temperature, pH below 7 is acidic, above 7 basic, about 7 neutral. Colour alone needs the appropriate chart. Indicator estimates do not establish chemical identity or safety. Prepare samples before class; avoid coloured/flavoured vinegar that obscures colour.

items.title: What an acid/base model explains
items.student: Evidence cards for reading, not experiments on bodies: A stomach acid supports digestion, but excessive acid may be neutralised by a suitable antacid base. Carbon dioxide made during respiration can dissolve in water and make it more acidic. Many chlorine bleaches are alkaline, but their colour-removing action is oxidation of coloured substances, not a general property of all bases. In a simple aqueous model acids increase H+ (more fully hydrated as H3 O+) and soluble hydroxide bases supply OH−; not every base is a soluble hydroxide. Match each process to a role and state one limit of the model.
items.teacher: Explain the aqueous model without claiming all bases directly releaseOH− or all neutralisations give pH7. Antacid is an explanatory example, not an instruction to take medicine. No bleach, bodily fluids or breath-sharing experiments. Bleach/acid mixing can release hazardous chlorine gas. Teacher references: RSC microscale acid/base activities; University of Bristol hypochlorite explanations. Detailed sources are in sources/science_references.json.

items.title: A base neutralises acid
items.student: Teacher demonstration after local risk assessment: use a tray, goggles, dropper, stirrer and universal-indicator paper. Put 2 mL of the prepared 0.1 mol/L hydrochloric acid in a small open well or beaker. Add prepared 0.1 mol/L sodium hydroxide in small drops, stirring and testing on fresh indicator paper. Stop at approximately neutral indication, then add a small excess to a separate matched trial. Learners record direction of pH change. Learners do not prepare or handle concentrated reagents. Fallback qualitative evidence card: initial acid pH1; near-balanced mixture pH7; excess alkali pH10 (illustrative, not measured).
items.teacher: For HCl andNaOH: hydrochloric acid+sodium hydroxide→sodium chloride+water. H++OH−→water is the particle-level simplification. Near-equal volumes are expected only because these particular solutions have equal concentration and 1: 1 reaction. Do not generalise equal volumes to every acid/base. No evaporation or heating. Teacher controls solutions and disposes of material under school policy; pH testing is required before any approved drain disposal.

items.title: Acid and a carbonate
items.student: Class microscale activity only after teacher approval: each pair has an open cup on a tray with 2 mL diluted food vinegar, one small pre-measured pinch (about 0.1 g) sodium bicarbonate, a spatula and goggles. Add the powder slowly; observe without capping the container. Record bubbling. Never taste or test a gas with a flame. Alternative evidence: bubbles form when the two named reagents mix. Use the information “acid+carbonate→salt+water+carbon dioxide” to identify products; discuss why bubbles alone cannot identify a gas.
items.teacher: Bicarbonate (hydrogen carbonate) is used as an accessible related example: vinegar(acetic acid)+sodium hydrogen carbonate→sodium acetate+water+carbon dioxide. Explain this naming distinction. For a carbonate example on paper: hydrochloric acid+calcium carbonate→calcium chloride+water+carbon dioxide. Bubbling indicates gas evolution, not gas identity by itself. Allow time for cleanup; teacher supplies and collects all materials.

items.title: Acid and a metal
items.student: Teacher-only microscale demonstration in a ventilated laboratory: put one small magnesium-ribbon piece (about 2 mm) in an open well on a tray; add 2 drops of prepared 1 mol/L hydrochloric acid. Teacher and observers wear goggles and keep a safe viewing distance. Observe bubbles and the metal becoming smaller. No flame, gas collection or sealed vessel. No nitric acid or other metal is substituted. If the teacher cannot provide the setting and approved risk assessment, use the observation card instead: magnesium gets smaller and a gas forms.
items.teacher: Magnesium+hydrochloric acid→magnesium chloride+hydrogen. The named reactants and established reaction model identify the gas; the bubbles alone do not. Magnesium is flammable and hydrogen is flammable: remove ignition sources. This is a narrowed adaptation of the RSC microscale acid-metal activity, not its full multi-acid procedure. Local teacher confirms reagent availability, cleanup and disposal. Evidence-card work does not demonstrate hands-on practical competence.

items.title: Three salts exchange water with air
items.student: Illustrative comparison, not real measured data: each labelled salt starts at 5.00 g under its stated conditions, then is exposed to air. Salt A ends at 5.30 g and remains a solid; Salt B ends at 6.20 g and forms a solution; Salt C is a hydrated salt; it ends at 4.20 g and becomes powdery. For this comparison the only mass transfer is water. Calculate mass change and classify each behaviour. What evidence would you need before applying this explanation to an unknown powder?
items.teacher: A takes up 0.30 g water: hygroscopic.B takes up 1.20 g and dissolves: deliquescent(a special hygroscopic behaviour).C loses 0.80 g water: efflorescent if the lost water is water of crystallisation. These are conditioned illustrative cases, not substance-identification tests. Appearance alone cannot establish identity, chemical safety or purity. Humidity and temperature affect whether and how fast changes occur.

items.title: Prepare a fair exposure comparison
items.student: Teacher demonstration or prepared samples: clearly labelled small samples of calcium chloride and sodium carbonate decahydrate(washing soda), kept in separate trays out of reach. Teacher prepares an exposed and a covered comparison of each in advance, records time and room conditions, and photographs or weighs them. Learners use observations supplied by the teacher; no handling or heating. Decide which comparisons are fair and whether the evidence supports water gain or loss. If samples or balances are unavailable, use G7 only and mark this as data interpretation.
items.teacher: Calcium chloride can absorb enough atmospheric water to form solution; washing-soda crystals can lose water of crystallisation. Outcomes depend on air conditions, so never promise a visible result within 40 minutes. The teacher checks supplier safety data and uses goggles; avoid dust, skin contact and heat released when calcium chloride contacts water. Do not add water or mix the salts. Keep prepared samples away from food; dispose under school policy. This lesson assesses planning and interpretation, not an assured same-lesson transformation.

items.title: Useful salts and responsible use
items.student: Read the application cards: food-grade sodium chloride is used in food; fertiliser salts supply nutrients to crops; some medicines contain salts; washing soda is used in laundry. Excess fertiliser nutrients reaching water can contribute to eutrophication. Excess dietary sodium is associated with raised blood pressure, but sodium also has necessary body functions. Create a classroom information poster with(a)one useful application,(b)one environmental or health concern,(c)one safe-use action. Include a separate “never mix cleaners” message. Where a device and an approved offline or online source are available, find one supporting statement and record its source; otherwise use the supplied printed G11 source-summary card and mark digital research as not observed. This is school-based education, no medical advice or actual community distribution.
items.teacher: Keep “salt” as a chemical class distinct from only table salt. Food-grade and dose/context matter; not all salts are edible. For health use WHO sodium-reduction evidence; give no individual intake target or treatment. Accept reading labels, avoiding unnecessary added salt, preventing fertiliser runoff or following trained advice as context-appropriate messages. Teacher checks wording before any later public sharing. Outcome f is assessed through a reasoned action, not agreement with a personal opinion.

items.title: Independent assessment evidence
items.student: All numbers are illustrative. Aqueous solutions P, Q, R have approximate indicator pH3, 8, 7 near room temperature. A5.00 g sample ends at 5.80 g and forms a solution after exposure to air; another 5.00 g hydrated sample ends at 4.50 g and becomes powdery, with water the only exchanged material. A laboratory record names dilute hydrochloric acid and magnesium; another names hydrochloric acid and calcium carbonate. Use these data with the unit’s reaction and safe-use models.
items.teacher: Full key is in the Final Explanation teacher document. This assessment uses evidence, not additional laboratory work. Responses must distinguish observations from inferred products and must not identify pH as a general safety test.

items.title: Printed source summaries for responsible use
items.student: Use this printed source card when digital access is unavailable. These are paraphrased classroom notes, checked 12 November 2026, not complete copies of the source pages. WHO explains that sodium is needed for normal body functions, while excess dietary sodium is linked to higher blood pressure. Reading food labels and avoiding unnecessary added salt are general information points, not a personal treatment or intake target. The US Environmental Protection Agency explains that excess nitrogen and phosphorus in water can increase algal growth and harm water ecosystems. University of Bristol explains that hypochlorite bleach acts by oxidation; bleach mixed with acids can release hazardous chlorine. Never mix cleaners. Sources: WHO, Sodium reduction: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/sodium-reduction ; US EPA, The problem: https://www.epa.gov/nutrientpollution/problem ; University of Bristol, Sodium Hypochlorite (Bleach): https://www.chm.bris.ac.uk/motm/bleach/Sodium%20Hypochlorite%20-%20Molecule%20of%20the%20Month%20October%202011.pdf . Select one statement relevant to your G9 poster, name the source, and explain how it supports your safe-use action.
items.teacher: Provide G11 as the printed reference for G9. This supplies an attributed statement without requiring a live device. Mark source reading as demonstrated where justified; mark digital research as not observed when only this printed card is used. Check every poster before sharing, and do not infer personal medical or fertiliser dosing advice.
